evidence.claim: New York renumbered its Troy-to-Massachusetts highway as Route 2 in 1942.
evidence.quote: In 1942, the state of New York switched the alignments of NY 96 and NY 2, a highway extending from Owego to Rochester in the Finger Lakes region. The change placed NY 2 on the Troy–Massachusetts routing.

evidence.claim: Williamstown’s 1753 House dates from 1953.
evidence.quote: The 1753 House was built in 1953 to help celebrate the 200th anniversary of the town's founding.

evidence.claim: Volunteers used eighteenth-century materials and tools to build the replica for the town’s bicentennial celebration.
evidence.quote: Built by volunteers using 18th-century building materials and tools, the replica house is intended to recreate how a typical home is believed to have looked back in 1753.

evidence.claim: The town’s name has a separate story: Ephraim Williams left money on condition that the town bear his name and establish a free school.
evidence.quote: He bequeathed a significant sum to the town on the condition that the town would be named after him and that a free school would be established.

evidence.claim: The town was incorporated under the Williamstown name in 1765, following Williams’s will; its earlier name was West Hoosac.
evidence.quote: The town was incorporated in 1765 as Williamstown according to the will of Col. Ephraim Williams

evidence.claim: That school opened in 1791 and became Williams College in 1793.
evidence.quote: In 1791 the school opened but only lasted a short time as a free school. It became Williams College in 1793.

evidence.claim: The college remains in Williamstown, where the town center lies southwest of the Green and Hoosic rivers’ confluence.

evidence.claim: Petersburg Pass once had a ski lodge and parking lots beside the height of land on New York Route 2.
evidence.quote: Originally known as Petersburg Pass Ski Area, the base lodge and parking lots were located adjacent to the height of land on New York State Route 2.

evidence.claim: The ski area opened in 1962 with a double chairlift, then added a novice lift in 1964.
evidence.quote: Started in 1962, the ski area featured a variety of trails served by a Poma double chairlift.  A novice surface lift was added below the base area in 1964.

evidence.claim: The steep road approach and a shortage of snowmaking water contributed to its difficulties.
evidence.quote: Due to a variety of reasons, including the steep ascent up Route 2 and the lack of water for snowmaking, the ski area struggled through much of its existence.

evidence.claim: It missed several seasons in the 1970s and closed in 1980, leaving an attempted expansion on Mount Raimer’s western face unfinished.
evidence.quote: An attempt was made to dramatically expand the ski area during its final years, as trails were cut on the western face of the mountain.  This expansion was never completed and the ski area went out of business in 1980.

evidence.claim: It missed several seasons in the 1970s and closed in 1980, leaving an attempted expansion on Mount Raimer’s western face unfinished.

evidence.claim: Attempts to revive the business included two name changes, first to Taconic Trails and then Mount Raimer; its double chairlift was later sold to Ski Butternut.
evidence.quote: After a short time as Taconic Trails, the ski area was last known as Mount Raimer.
